transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-08-05
Start: 2026-08-05T15:00:00Z
Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Jules Kramer (Product), Aisha Barnes (CTO - LumenWorks), Tom Reyes (Head of Platform), Derek Luo (SRE), Nia Gomez (Security)

Auto Summary (auto-generated): Quick console walkthrough focusing on tracing and request playback. Several questions about private deployment and audit logs. Agreed to POC scoping and share security docs.

[00:00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, i think we've got most folks — hi aisha, hi tom, hello derek — we'll run through the console sleuthing playbook, show how traces and request logs map to token-level cost and then open for q's, sound good?
[00:00:19] Aisha Barnes: yep sounds great, we want to see the actual flow end to end cause our ops team wants reproducible debugging, not just opaque logs.
[00:00:34] Ravi Patel: perfect — i'll share my screen, bear with me — ok i'm in the redwood console, this is the request inspector that ties request ids to model route, node, and kv cache hits. sometimes the OCR transcriber calls it request "inspector" or "insector" in notes, ignore that haha.
[00:00:58] Tom Reyes: quick question — you said kv cache hits, do we get visibility into prefix cache evictions? that's been a black box for us on our current stack.
[00:01:12] Ravi Patel: yes, we show per-request kv stats: hit/miss, cache key fingerprint, approximate memory used. evictions are correlatable by timestamp; we also surface a short histogram of sequence lengths which drives cache usefulness.
[00:01:33] Derek Luo: is that only for hosted or also for dedicated/private nodes? we run in a VPC and need the same telemetry.
[00:01:45] Maya Chen: good point — the observability surfaces are consistent across hosted and dedicated; for private we can stream logs to their S3 endpoint or syslog and keep the console for the control plane.
[00:02:03] Nia Gomez: and audit logs — do you retain user-level actions and key rotation events? our compliance needs a three-year audit trail ideally.
[00:02:17] Jules Kramer: short answer, yes — we have audit logs, key rotation meta, and we integrate with KMS/HSM providers. retention configurable for private. for hosted we have default retention windows, and enterprise add-on for long term.
[00:02:35] Aisha Barnes: can you demo a tricky error flow — like when a request falls back to a cheaper quantized variant but latencies spike, and how we triage that?
[00:02:50] Ravi Patel: great example — i'll inject a synthetic request. watch the trace: top lane is routing decision, next lane is model variant chosen, then worker node latency, then token stream.
[00:03:12] [Screen share: request trace id 0x4a9f]
[00:03:14] Ravi Patel: see here, routing policy tried the primary variant gptx-16b-fp16 but capacity was low so it fell back to gptx-16b-int8 with a different kernel. notice the increased step latency at token 42 — that's where quantization kernel got a bad memory page alignment on this infra, it adds jitter.
[00:03:40] Tom Reyes: hmm we saw similar in our tests — does redwood surface kernel selection and which CUDA/cu* kernel was used? we need that to correlate to NV driver versions.
[00:03:53] Ravi Patel: yes we surface kernel family and approximated kernel version, plus a link to node metadata so you can match to driver/AMI. occasionally the console will show slightly off names, e.g., it might show "cudaExec_v2" instead of exact vendor name because of our aggregation, but you can get the node id and check infra.
[00:04:15] Aisha Barnes: what's the span granularity? we need to trace across batching boundaries — our requests are often batched at 16 concurrent.
[00:04:28] Ravi Patel: we tag spans with batch id and token offset. the playback tool can replay the exact request slice that went into a batch; you can replay single-request or entire batch to a sandboxed endpoint for repro.
[00:04:46] Derek Luo: playback — can that be replayed against a pinned model version? we want to test regressions.
[00:04:55] Ravi Patel: yes, playback supports model pinning and rollbacks. we also keep a delta report on output diffs between versions. note the diffs are helpful but non-determinism in sampling can cause noise — we add deterministic seeds when capturing evals.
[00:05:13] [00:05:13] Tom Reyes: the console UI here — is there an API to pull traces into our own splunk/datadog?
[00:05:23] Jules Kramer: absolutely — we have a traces export API and a webhook sink. many customers push to datadog; we can share example parsers.
[00:05:37] Maya Chen: i'll drop a link after the call to the traces export docs, and a sample datadog mapping.
[00:05:46] Aisha Barnes: ok show us an error scenario where the model returns a malformed JSON for a function call and how we locate the prompt cause.
[00:05:58] Ravi Patel: good one — i'm filtering for function-output errors. here you can see token-level probabilities suppressed for trailing tokens because the system prompt had an unterminated bracket. the console highlights probable prompt issues and allows you to view the exact prompt as reconstructed from kv-cache + prefix.
[00:06:20] Derek Luo: sometimes the transcription here says "kv-kash" in earlier exports, hope you fixed that ;)
[00:06:30] Ravi Patel: haha yeah we fight the auto-tagger sometimes.
[00:06:34] Tom Reyes: about cost — how do we map tokens to dollar spend per request so product teams can prioritize expensive flows?
[00:06:45] Jules Kramer: per-route token accounting is supported. we show estimated cost per request and per token, and you can slice by model variant or by customer namespace. there is also a cost-heatmap to surface hot prompts.
[00:07:02] Aisha Barnes: and can that be attributed to feature flags or microservice caller? our call chain crosses an edge service and a vector-search microservice.
[00:07:13] Ravi Patel: yes, the platform supports route tags and caller identity. if your edge service sets a caller-id header we persist that in the trace. you can then aggregate costs by caller-id.
[00:07:26] [00:07:26] Nia Gomez: security question — for private deployments, can we enforce SSO-only access to the console and limit which engineers can call the replay feature?
[00:07:38] Maya Chen: yep role-based access controls, SAML/SSO, and granular console permissioning for playback and data export. for private we also offer an option to disable playback to hosted endpoints entirely.
[00:07:54] Tom Reyes: do you support encrypted-at-rest for cache blobs, like the KV cache? we need that for regs.
[00:08:05] Jules Kramer: KV cache can be encrypted via KMS — for private you can bring-your-own-key; for hosted we manage key rotation unless you opt into a customer-managed key.
[00:08:17] Aisha Barnes: can we see an incident postmortem example in the console? how are logs packaged?
[00:08:27] Ravi Patel: sure — here is an incident trace where a routing policy mis-routed to a deprecated variant. the console bundles a diagnostic package: trace JSON, node-level metrics, kernel dumps, and the route decision tree. we also have a one-click export to S3 for e-discovery.
[00:08:48] Derek Luo: do those packages include PII redaction options? our logs sometimes contain user prompts with emails.
[00:08:58] Jules Kramer: yes we support scrubbers and redaction rules prior to export. redaction can be applied at ingest or on-demand before sharing.
[00:09:12] [00:09:12] Maya Chen: want to circle back to fallback policies — a common design is cost-tiered fallbacks: primary -> warmed dedicated -> shared cheap. can we show policy config?
[00:09:26] Ravi Patel: yep policy editor here. you can set latency SLO thresholds, cost gates, and route weights. the console will simulate traffic and give projected cost impact before you apply.
[00:09:42] Tom Reyes: does the simulator account for kv cache hit rate? our workloads have high prefix reuse.
[00:09:51] Ravi Patel: it does — you can feed an empirical histogram or live sample and the sim will infer cache hit rates and estimate unit cost, often giving surprising savings with small cache tweaks.
[00:10:06] Aisha Barnes: anything about observability retention and how long traces are kept?
[00:10:14] Jules Kramer: retention configurable by plan; enterprise private can set long-term retention to match compliance. for hosted we provide tiers; if you need three years we recommend private or add-on.
[00:10:27] [00:10:27] Maya Chen: ok quick pause — any blockers or must-haves for you all before we scope a POC?
[00:10:36] Tom Reyes: must-haves: ability to run within our AWS account (VPC), KMS BYOK, and per-request playback disabled for some teams.
[00:10:46] Nia Gomez: plus SOC2 type II report and penetration test summary.
[00:10:52] Aisha Barnes: timeline wise, we want a POC in the next 3 weeks if possible.
[00:10:59] Maya Chen: we can move fast — i'll send draft POC plan after this call.
[00:11:05] [00:11:05] Ravi Patel: now i'll show a deeper troubleshooting pattern — when you have noisy latency you start with the trace, then inspect node-level GPU metrics and kernel timing. here's an example where a node had a scheduled maintenance and the driver mismatch caused timeouts for a short window.
[00:11:28] Tom Reyes: how do you correlate infra autoscaler events? sometimes autoscaling causes brief bursts of cold-start latencies.
[00:11:38] Ravi Patel: we capture autoscaler events and surface them in the trace timeline, and we annotate cold starts with a "warmth" metric. you can filter traces for cold-start occurrences.
[00:11:51] Derek Luo: can we get alerts on certain trace patterns? like repeated function-output failure rate crossing threshold?
[00:11:59] Jules Kramer: yes alerting integrated into console; we support webhooks, pagerduty, and datadog events. you can define alert rules on error-rate per route, cost anomalies, or latency SLOs.
[00:12:12] [00:12:12] Aisha Barnes: show us the playback UX one more time — i want to see the exact inputs we can replay.
[00:12:20] Ravi Patel: sure — selecting a trace shows the reconstructed prompt (merged from prefix, user, and system), the exact headers, and the kv snapshot. choose "replay" -> select target (sandbox dedicated) -> set deterministic seed -> run.
[00:12:36] Tom Reyes: do we need special credentials to hit your sandbox for POC? we'd rather have the runs in our own project.
[00:12:44] Maya Chen: for POC we can provision a short-lived dedicated cluster in your AWS account with terraform, that way you keep telemetry and keys.
[00:12:55] Nia Gomez: can we audit who replayed what? we need that to be auditable.
[00:13:02] Jules Kramer: replay events are logged in the audit trail with user id, timestamp, and target. again you can disable replay for users or roles.
[00:13:15] [00:13:15] Ravi Patel: i'm going to pull up an example where a prompt drifted after a model update — the delta report shows both outputs and highlights token-level divergence. for SREs, the combined view with cost and latency helps prioritize whether to roll back or to tune prompts.
[00:13:38] Aisha Barnes: we have a concern: some costs spiked unexpectedly when we started using function-calling heavily. can console attribute cost to function-call token overhead?
[00:13:50] Ravi Patel: yes, function-calls are attributed as part of the token accounting; you can group tokens by role (system, user, assistant, function call) and see per-role cost.
[00:14:03] Tom Reyes: about model variants — how do you handle consistency for hallucination-sensitive flows? fallback to smaller models reduces cost but increases hallucination risk. can policies include quality gates?
[00:14:16] Jules Kramer: policies can include quality monitors tied to prompt sets. you can configure a regression alert if output quality metrics drop below a threshold during a rollout and automatically rollback. we integrate evaluations into the rollout flow.
[00:14:31] [00:14:31] Derek Luo: do you have examples of automated fallback policies that we can copy?
[00:14:38] Ravi Patel: yes in our runbook library — i'll share a link after call with a couple of templates: latency-first, cost-first, and hybrid.
[00:14:48] Maya Chen: note, i'll include those in the follow-up email plus a POC template.
[00:14:55] [00:14:55] Aisha Barnes: any gotchas for multi-region traffic? we need global fallbacks and region-based routing.
[00:15:05] Jules Kramer: smart routing supports region affinity and automatic cross-region failover; we also show region-specific perf so you can set per-region SLOs.
[00:15:17] Tom Reyes: OK — i'd like us to test the worst-case trace: 1k concurrent QPS with 2k token average — how do you recommend we bench that?
[00:15:27] Ravi Patel: we recommend a staged approach: small ramp -> 5-minute sustained -> 30-minute ramp -> 24h soak. we can provide a harness and run it in your account, stream metrics into your datadog.
[00:15:40] [00:15:40] Maya Chen: any other security blockers?
[00:15:45] Nia Gomez: just the SOC2 and pen test artifacts, plus need to see KMS integration docs.
[00:15:52] Maya Chen: we'll include those.
[00:15:55] [Screen pause for Q&A 15:55-26:00 — rapid questions about RBAC and retention]
[00:26:05] Ravi Patel: quick note on debugging noisy sampling: console includes per-token log probs and top-K alternatives so you can see if the model had low confidence and why it chose certain tokens. that helps with hallucinations.
[00:26:23] Tom Reyes: can we add guardrails in the request layer to cap token generation for certain callers?
[00:26:31] Jules Kramer: yes request quotas and token caps per caller-id or API key are supported.
[00:26:41] Aisha Barnes: last question — if we go private, what's expected on our infra side? network peering, VPC endpoints?
[00:26:51] Maya Chen: typical requirements: a peered VPC or private link, an S3 bucket for logs if you want, and an IAM role for provisioning. we'll supply terraform that creates the infra as needed.
[00:27:03] Tom Reyes: timeline — you said POC in 3 weeks. what do you need from us to start?
[00:27:10] Maya Chen: ideal: traffic profile, a list of 5-10 golden prompts to monitor, compliance contact, and a sandbox account/role we can provision.
[00:27:21] Aisha Barnes: we'll compile that and send.
[00:27:24] [00:27:24] Maya Chen: ok i'll recap after this: next steps, links to docs, and who owns what. thanks for the questions, this was super helpful.
[00:27:33] Tom Reyes: thank you, appreciated the depth.
[00:27:37] Derek Luo: thanks everyone.
[00:27:40] Nia Gomez: thanks.

End of transcript (note: timestamps are approximate; some micro-timestamps collapsed).

References shared during call: https://redwood.ai/docs/traces-export (traces export docs), https://redwood.ai/security/soc2 (security whitepaper), https://example.s3/redwood/runbooks/policies (runbook samples)
